```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Every stage of harnessr except one is a pure function of its input. Extraction,
cleaning, segmentation, ranking and merging give the same result every time. The
model call is the only step that costs money, the only step that can die halfway
through a long run, and, above a temperature of zero, the only step that does
not return the same thing twice.

This guide covers what harnessr does about that: what a run records, the limits
every request is checked against before it is sent, the cache that makes a
repeat free, and the replay that reproduces a run from its trace with no key and
no spend. `vignette("harnessr")` introduces the package and its ideas.

## Setting up

The examples run offline. `gr_mock_client()` plays the part of the model, and
`embedder = "lexical"` gives free, deterministic word-overlap vectors in place of
an embeddings endpoint.

A mock costs nothing, which would leave every limit below with nothing to count.
So the examples give it a price: `gr_register_model()` registers a model id at
$2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens, and each run names
that model, so every request is priced at those rates.

```{r message = FALSE}
library(harnessr)

gr_register_model("priced-mock", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 2, output_usd = 8)
old <- gr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")

cl <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")
```

## What a run records

Everything below is recorded on the answer, and `print(ans)` sums it up: the
cost, where the evidence came from and, when the answer is partial, why.

```{r}
ans <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                       client = cl, model = "priced-mock", max_tokens = 150)
ans
```

Check `ans$partial` first. `TRUE` means something degraded, and `ans$notes` says
what: `dropped_chunks`, `failed_calls`, `unread_pages`, `call_cap_reached`,
`cost_cap_reached` and so on. `ans$warnings` holds every warning raised while the
document was read.

The trace holds every request the run made. `gr_trace_summary()` gives the
totals, `gr_trace_cost()` the bill by model, and `as.data.frame()` one row per
request with its stage, tokens, cost, time, prompt and reply:

```{r}
gr_trace_summary(ans$trace)[, c("calls", "cached", "tokens_in", "tokens_out", "errors")]
gr_trace_cost(ans$trace)[, c("model", "calls", "paid_calls", "usd")]
as.data.frame(ans$trace)[, c("step", "stage", "tokens_in", "tokens_out", "usd")]
```

The token totals are the size of the prompts and replies, which is the shape of
a run, not its bill. `gr_trace_cost()` counts only the calls that were issued: a
call answered from a cache or a recording spent nothing, however long its
prompt. A model with no registered price contributes `NA`, never 0, so a total
cannot quietly leave one out.

You can also ask what a run would cost before you make it:

```{r}
gr_estimate_cost("priced-mock", input_tokens = 120000, output_tokens = 4000)
```

### What each request records

Each request is one entry in `trace$steps`. Besides its label, prompt, reply and
the model it asked for, a step records:

- `params`, what the call asked for, and `params_sent`, the request as it went
  out with every default resolved: the model, `api`, `base_url`, the output cap
  sent, the temperature (`NA` when none was sent), the effort, the
  schema name, and SHA-256 hashes of the JSON schema and of any extra body
  fields. A reasoning model's small cap goes out raised to 2048, and
  `params_sent` shows the raised one.
- `served_model`, `response_id` and `fingerprint`, where the provider returns
  them. `model` stays the model asked for, which is what the step is priced and
  replayed by.
- `attempts`, the number of requests sent, retries included (0 for a reply from
  a cache or a recording), and `started_utc` and `ended_utc` in ISO 8601 UTC.
- `tokens`, with `provenance`: `"reported"` by the provider, `"counted"` here
  with the `"tiktoken"` tokenizer, or `"estimated"` with another one. Reasoning
  and cached input tokens the provider reports are kept as `tokens$reasoning`
  and `tokens$cached_input`, as parts of `output` and `input` rather than
  additions.

```{r}
step <- ans$trace$steps[[length(ans$trace$steps)]]
str(step[c("label", "attempts", "started_utc", "tokens")])
str(step$params_sent)
```

A mock reports no usage, so its counts are estimated. `gr_trace_summary()`
gives the share of requests whose counts were estimated as `usage_estimated`,
and `print()` on a trace says so when it is above zero.

`refine` and `hierarchical` also record the length of the state they carry
forward. Each `refine.draft` and `refine.revise` step has `state$tokens_in`, the
draft the request carried, and `state$tokens_out`, the draft carried on from it
(the old one when the reply was unusable). Each `hier.summarise.L<k>` step has
the length of the text it summarised and of the summary it returned, and each
level adds a local `hier.state.L<k>` step with the number of summaries handed on
and their combined length. A draft that shrinks sharply in one revision shows up
there.

Every cut made to fit a limit writes a local `truncate` step with where it was
made (`detail$where`), the token limit, and the tokens before, kept and dropped.
`refine` and `hierarchical` answers add the tokens cut as
`notes$tokens_truncated`, and printing one says how many tokens were cut to fit.
Here a model with a 1,000-token window makes `refine` cut its growing draft:

```{r}
gr_register_model("small-window", context_window = 1000, max_output = 500,
                  input_usd = 2, output_usd = 8)
long_draft <- paste(rep("Revenue was 45.2 million dollars, and the draft says so.", 30),
                    collapse = " ")
cut <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "fast",
                       client = gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) long_draft),
                       reader = "refine", model = "small-window",
                       max_tokens = 120, max_answer_tokens = 200)
cuts <- Filter(function(s) identical(s$label, "truncate"), cut$trace$steps)
str(cuts[[1]]$detail)
cut$notes$tokens_truncated
```

The other places a cut can be made are `refine.excerpt`, `hier.summaries`,
`preview.skim`, `preview.outline`, `<label>.input` for a finding cut to fit a
merge, `<label>.giveup` for the capped findings a failed merge returns,
`segment.contextual.header`, `segment.contextual.document`, `screen.opening`,
`synthesise.gaps` and `embed.input`.

A trace also records who the run is for and what it ran under. `gr_trace()`
takes `system`, `owner`, `run_by`, `purpose` and `approved_by`, and
`gr_options(actor = list(...))` sets them for every trace; a field named nowhere
is `NA`. `trace$config` is a snapshot of the options in force when the trace was
made, with the R version. The values of `api_headers` are left out, since they
can hold credentials.

```{r}
tr <- gr_trace(owner = "finance team", run_by = "ana", purpose = "Q3 check")
tr
names(tr$config)
```

`as_json(ans)` writes the answer with every prompt and response from the same
run, and `gr_trace_save()` writes the trace alone, which is what a replay reads.

### Errors and warnings by class

Errors are classed, so you can catch a specific failure: `gr_auth_error`,
`gr_file_not_found`, `gr_empty_document`, `gr_unsupported_format`,
`gr_overflow`, `gr_call_cap`, `gr_cost_cap`, `gr_budget_error`,
`gr_unknown_model`, `gr_unknown_override`, `gr_no_recipes`, `gr_bad_ensemble`,
`gr_missing_dep`, `gr_bad_setting` for a setting outside its choices
(`vignette("extending")`), `hr_unknown_effort_key` and `hr_unpriced_model`
(both below), and `hr_dim_mismatch` when two vectors of different lengths are
compared, such as a lexical fallback vector against an API embedding.
Degradations are classed warnings: `gr_segment_fallback`, `gr_embed_fallback`,
`gr_rerank_degraded`, `gr_iterative_degraded`, `gr_ensemble_degenerate`,
`gr_duplicate_recipe`, `gr_deprecated`, `gr_ocr_unavailable`, `gr_clamped` with
`hr_param_clamped` for a parameter moved to its nearest bound
(`vignette("extending")`), `gr_parallel_share` for a parallel item whose
share refused a later request (below), `gr_bad_correct` for a
`gr_compare()` `correct` function that fails (below), and `gr_unclear_dropped`
when `gr_extract()` leaves unclear screening records out (`vignette("review")`).

In an interactive session a long read keeps one line up to date with how many
chunks it has read and what it has spent, and `gr_read_many()` gives the spend
so far before each document.

## Limits

Two limits are on by default: a run may spend $5 and make 400 calls.

```{r}
unlist(gr_options()[c("max_cost_usd", "max_calls")])
```

They are checked twice. Before the first request, a run is refused with a
classed error naming the option to change when it would need more calls than
`max_calls`, or when its reader sends every chunk and sending them would already
cost more than `max_cost_usd`. Here `map_reduce` over five chunks needs six
calls:

```{r}
chunks <- gr_segment(gr_example(), list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 150))
spec <- gr_read_spec(reader = "map_reduce", model = "priced-mock")

tryCatch(
  gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue?", cl, spec,
          trace = gr_trace(governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 3))),
  gr_call_cap = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

### Every request is checked before it is sent

Then every request is checked before it goes out, against what the run has spent
plus the most the request could cost: its prompt at the input price and its
output cap at the output price. The prompt is counted with the JSON schema and
extra body fields the request carries and a few tokens of framing per message,
then raised by `safety_margin`, since the provider bills for all of that. A
request that could take the run past a limit is not sent, so a run ends at or
under its limit rather than one request over it.

Under a limit of one cent, the five chunk requests below go out and the merge
does not. Its reply cap is 1500 tokens, which at $8 per million could cost more
than the run has left, so the answer comes back partial:

```{r}
tr <- gr_trace(governor = hr_governor(max_cost_usd = 0.01))
capped <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue?", cl, spec, trace = tr)
capped$partial
data.frame(calls = tr$calls, spent_usd = tr$spent_usd, stop_reason = tr$stop_reason)
tr$refusals[[1]]$message
```

The bound rests on two things harnessr cannot see: that the provider stops each
reply at its cap, and that it counts the prompt within `safety_margin` of the
local tokenizer. A run that leaves its output caps at the model's limit stops
while it still has headroom a smaller cap would have used. With the merge's reply
held to 500 tokens, the same run fits:

```{r}
tr <- gr_trace(governor = hr_governor(max_cost_usd = 0.01))
fits <- gr_read(chunks, "What was revenue?", cl,
                gr_read_spec(reader = "map_reduce", model = "priced-mock",
                             max_answer_tokens = 500),
                trace = tr)
fits$partial
data.frame(calls = tr$calls, spent_usd = tr$spent_usd)
```

A refused request is not a call. It adds nothing to the trace's calls, steps or
spend. `gr_call()` returns it as a failed result with `refused = TRUE` and an
error naming the limit, after signalling a condition of class
`hr_budget_refused`, which you can catch to stop instead. The trace lists it in
`refusals`, sets `budget_stop` and names the limit in `stop_reason`: `"calls"`,
`"cost"`, `"tokens"`, `"output"`, `"model"` or `"unpriced"`. Readers and review
stages mark the answer or section partial and do not count the request as
failed.

The check sits on the call path itself, so it covers every request: readers,
judges, the ensemble's adjudication, conflict resolution in `gr_extract()`,
context and proposition segmentation, claims, outlines, screening, synthesis,
embeddings, and any request a custom reader or a script makes with `gr_call()`.

### A governor for one run

`hr_governor()` holds a run's limits. Attach one with `gr_trace(governor = )`;
a trace without one reads the limits from `gr_options()` each time it checks.
It has six:

| limit | what it holds | default |
|---|---|---|
| `max_calls` | requests the run may make, cache hits and embeddings included | 400 |
| `max_cost_usd` | what the run may spend, in USD | 5 |
| `max_tokens_total` | tokens of every prompt, reply and embedded text | off |
| `max_output_tokens` | the largest output cap one request may carry; a request with a larger one is refused, not cut down | off |
| `allowed_models` | the model ids the run may call, text and embedding models alike | any |
| `allow_unpriced` | whether a model with no registered price may be called under a spending limit | `FALSE` |

Each is also an option of the same name, so `gr_options(max_tokens_total = 50000)`
sets it for every run, and each trace's config snapshot lists them all. `NULL`
or `Inf` removes a limit. A limit that cannot be compared is refused when you
set it:

```{r}
tryCatch(gr_options(max_cost_usd = NA), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

A request to a model the run may not call is refused the same way as one over
budget:

```{r}
tr <- gr_trace(governor = hr_governor(allowed_models = "gpt-4o"))
res <- gr_call(cl, "What was revenue?", model = "priced-mock", trace = tr)
data.frame(refused = res$refused, stop_reason = tr$stop_reason)
```

`gr_read_many()`, `gr_claims()`, `gr_outline()` and `gr_synthesise()` keep a
trace of their own and fold it into the one they are given. They hold their
requests to that trace's governor, less what it has already spent and used in
tokens; `max_calls` stays a limit per document and per stage. `gr_compare()`
holds the whole comparison to `max_cost_usd` and `max_tokens_total`.

### Models with no price

A language model with no registered price adds nothing to the spend, so a
spending limit could never stop it. While `max_cost_usd` is set, a request to one is
refused with a condition of class `hr_unpriced_model`, and `gr_read()` stops
before its first request. `gr_backend_client()` wraps an R function as a paying
client, so it shows the refusal offline:

```{r}
gr_register_model("unpriced-model", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096)
backend <- gr_backend_client(function(messages, params) "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.")

res <- gr_call(backend, "What was revenue?", model = "unpriced-model")
res$refused
res$error
```

Register the model's prices with `gr_register_model()`, or set
`gr_options(allow_unpriced = TRUE)`. Then its requests are sent, still count
against `max_calls` and `max_tokens_total`, and are priced `NA` in the trace.
`max_tokens_total` is the limit that still bounds such a run. `gr_mock_client()`
and replays are never refused for this, and neither are embedding models with no
price.

A `gr_ellmer_client()` is priced as the model its ellmer object was built with,
whatever a recipe names, so one built on a model with no registered price is
refused too. Register that model at your provider's current prices, or let a
local model run unpriced; the README's "Connecting a model" section shows both.
Through ellmer, a `temperature` in a read spec is ignored with a warning,
because sampling parameters belong to the ellmer object, and embeddings come
from a function you pass as `embed =`; without one, `retrieve` and the
`semantic` segmenter fall back to lexical vectors and say so.

### Parallel batches

With `parallel = TRUE`, per-chunk requests go out in batches that cannot be
stopped part way. Each worker's items are held to an equal share of the calls
and dollars the run has left. If a worker's share refuses an item before it is
sent, the item is run again in the calling process against the run's own
limits. A batch the run's limits cannot cover is not split across workers; it
runs in the calling process. Batch items make one request each; an item that
made more and had a later one refused by its share warns with class
`gr_parallel_share`, and the run is not marked as stopped.

### How much the model reasons

`effort` sets how much a reasoning model reasons on each call, by stage;
`vignette("readers")` explains how it is billed, which models it is sent to,
and the label each stage's calls carry. In a review, the same vector goes to
each stage: `gr_screen()` and `gr_extract()` take it as a recipe override, and
`gr_claims()`, `gr_outline()` and `gr_synthesise()` take it as an argument, so
`effort = c(extract = "low", synthesise = "high")` keeps the per-chunk
extraction cheap and spends on the writing. A name that matches no declared call
stops with an error of class `hr_unknown_effort_key` that lists the stems, so a
misspelt `c(extrac = "low")` cannot send every extraction at the provider's
default unnoticed. `?gr_read_spec` lists every label and suggests a profile: low
for the many per-chunk calls, high for the few that judge.

## Paying once

`gr_cache()` stores each successful response, keyed on the exact request. A
repeat is free and identical:

```{r}
cache  <- gr_cache(file.path(tempdir(), "harnessr-runs-cache"))
cached <- gr_cache_client(cl, cache)

first  <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                          client = cached, model = "priced-mock")
second <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                          client = cached, model = "priced-mock")

gr_trace_summary(second$trace)[, c("calls", "cached", "tokens_in")]
gr_trace_cost(second$trace)[, c("calls", "paid_calls", "usd")]
```

`cached` counts the calls answered from the cache rather than the network, so
`calls - cached` is what the run paid for. The token counts stay, since that is
how big the prompts were, but a run with `cached == calls` cost nothing, so do
not hand its totals to `gr_estimate_cost()` and call the result a bill.

The key covers everything that can change the reply: the messages, the model,
the resolved output cap, the temperature, the JSON schema, the API shape and the
base URL. It does not cover the API key, the headers, the timeout or the retry
policy, none of which the model sees. If a header changes which model answers,
give that client its own `base_url` or `model` so the cache can tell them apart.
Failures are never cached: a rate limit or a refusal is a property of the
moment, and storing one would make a blip permanent. Neither is a reply cut off
at its output cap, or a structured reply that does not fit its schema, so
running again asks again.

The default directory is under `tempdir()`, so a cache costs nothing and
vanishes with the session. For a long run, point it somewhere real and the run
becomes resumable. Restart after a crash and every completed call is already
paid for:

```{r eval = FALSE}
gr_options(cache_dir = tools::R_user_dir("harnessr", "cache"))
```

`gr_cache_stats()` reports entries, bytes, hits, misses and writes, and
`gr_cache_clear()` empties a cache. Set `write = FALSE` to run against a frozen
cache, or `read = FALSE` to refresh entries already stored.

### Repeated draws

At a temperature above zero a cache hit replays one sample instead of drawing a
new one. That is what makes a run reproducible, but it also means N identical
calls are one draw N times, and anything that compares them sees perfect
agreement. To keep N draws, give each call its own `draw_index`. Above 0 it is
part of the key, so draws 1 to N are N entries, and a rerun gets the same N
replies back in the same order:

```{r}
n <- 0
sampler <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) { n <<- n + 1; paste("draw", n) })
sampler <- gr_cache_client(sampler, gr_cache(file.path(tempdir(), "harnessr-runs-draws")))

vapply(1:3, function(k) gr_call(sampler, "Pick one.", draw_index = k)$text, "")
vapply(1:3, function(k) gr_call(sampler, "Pick one.", draw_index = k)$text, "")
```

The second line is answered from the cache. A call with the default
`draw_index = 0` keys as an ordinary call always has. Use a fresh directory, or
`read = FALSE`, when you want new replies for draws already stored.

### Older caches

Entries are keyed by a SHA-256 hash under `harnessr-cache-v3`. Entries written
under the old key (`readgpt-cache-v2`, by readgpt 0.6.0 and earlier builds of
harnessr) are still read for calls with no draw index. The first reply found
that way in a session warns once, with class `hr_legacy_key`, and
`gr_cache_stats()` counts them as `legacy_hits`. Old entries are never
rewritten, and `gr_cache_clear()` removes both. With
`tools::R_user_dir("harnessr", "cache")` set, entries readgpt kept in
`tools::R_user_dir("readgpt", "cache")` are read too, after it.

## Replaying a run

A trace records every prompt and every response. That makes it a complete
transcript of the only non-deterministic part of the pipeline, so a trace plus
the source document reproduces a run exactly, with no key and no spend:

```{r}
f <- file.path(tempdir(), "run.json")
gr_trace_save(first$trace, f)

replayed <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "thorough",
                            client = gr_replay_client(f), model = "priced-mock")
identical(replayed$answer, first$answer)
```

Ship the trace next to the paper and a reader reproduces the run instead of
paying to approximate it. A trace file is also a re-runnable bug report: it
records exactly what went wrong.

A reply is matched on the key `harnessr-replay-v2`: the prompt messages, the
model the call asked for, its effort, its temperature once the session default
is filled in, the output cap asked for and its JSON schema. Each step records it
as `replay_key`. A prompt with no recorded reply raises `gr_replay_miss` rather
than inventing an answer. A miss means the replay has diverged from the
recording, and a result that looks like the original but is not is worse than no
replay at all. When the prompt was recorded under other settings, the message
names the recorded temperature, cap or schema next to the ones asked for. Pass
`strict = FALSE` to run a partial recording anyway.

A replay that asks for more replies than were recorded is an error too, of class
`hr_replay_exhausted`. Draw k of a request is answered with the reply recorded
for that draw:

```{r}
tr <- gr_trace()
n <- 0
sampler <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) { n <<- n + 1; paste("draw", n) })
invisible(lapply(1:3, function(k) gr_call(sampler, "Pick one.", draw_index = k, trace = tr)))

rp <- gr_replay_client(tr)
vapply(1:3, function(k) gr_call(rp, "Pick one.", draw_index = k)$text, "")
tryCatch(gr_call(rp, "Pick one.", draw_index = 4),
         hr_replay_exhausted = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

`gr_replay_client(on_exhausted = "flag")` repeats the last recorded reply
instead, which is what every replay did before, and counts each repeat in
`$stats()$repeats`. A step recorded before `replay_key` existed is looked up by
the old key, `readgpt-replay-v1` (messages, model and effort only), with one
`hr_legacy_key` warning per recording in a session.

### Embeddings in a replay

A trace records each embeddings request and what it cost, but not the vectors
that came back. A replay reproduces a run's chunk ranking exactly only when the
recording used a deterministic embedder and the replay uses the same one. Both
conditions, not either: replaying an API-embedded run with a deterministic local
embedder would compute vectors the original never saw while looking exact.
Anything else warns (`gr_replay_no_embeddings`) and falls back to lexical
vectors. Those place semantic cuts and rank chunks differently, so a replay of a
run that used embeddings (the `needle` recipe, the `retrieve` and `iterative`
readers, the `semantic` segmenter) usually sends prompts the recording does not
hold. A strict replay then stops with `gr_replay_miss`, whose message names this
cause.

Record a run you intend to publish with `gr_options(embedder = "lexical")`, as
this guide does, or with your own embedder registered as `deterministic = TRUE`:

```{r}
run <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "needle",
                       client = cl, model = "priced-mock")
again <- answer_document(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", "needle",
                         client = gr_replay_client(run$trace), model = "priced-mock")
identical(again$chunks_used, run$chunks_used)
```

### Limits in a replay

A saved trace says whether a limit cut the run short (`budget_stop`,
`stop_reason`), and a replay under the limits it was recorded with stops where
it stopped. Replayed calls count against `max_calls` as they did when recorded.
When the spending limit stopped the recorded run, each replayed call also counts
what it cost when recorded against `max_cost_usd`, in the trace's
`replayed_usd`, though nothing is spent; for any other run it counts nothing, so
a replay of an expensive run is not stopped by the replaying session's limit.
A replay under a higher limit that asks for a call past the recorded stop gets a
`gr_replay_miss` saying so.

Traces do not store the JSON schema a call requested, only a hash of it in the
step's key. In a recording made before `replay_key` existed, two calls that
differ only by schema, temperature or output cap share a reply.

## Comparing what recipes cost

`gr_compare()` runs several recipes over one document on one trace. Its
`summary` says what each recipe cost: `calls`, `tokens_in`, `tokens_out` and
`usd`, priced at each model's registered price, and `usd_estimated`, the share of
those dollars spent on requests whose token counts were estimated locally. Give
`correct`, strings a right answer contains or a function of each answer, and it
adds `correct` and `usd_per_correct`, the cost of a right answer:

```{r}
cmp <- gr_compare(gr_example(), "What was revenue?", c("fast", "precise", "thorough"),
                  client = cl, model = "priced-mock", correct = "45.2 million")
cmp$summary[, c("recipe", "reader", "calls", "usd", "usd_estimated",
                "correct", "usd_per_correct")]
```

`usd_per_correct` is `usd` for a right answer, `Inf` for a wrong one that cost
something, and `NA` when correctness is not known. A recipe a limit stopped
before it found anything is `NA`, not wrong. A recipe is charged for a
segmentation it shares with an earlier recipe, as it would be run alone, so the
column can add up to more than `gr_trace_cost(cmp$trace)`.

## Models, prices and token counts

`gr_models()` lists the context windows and prices harnessr knows, and
`gr_model_limits()` and `gr_model_info()` look one model up. Check them before
a long run: an unregistered model falls back to a conservative 128k window with
no price, so its cost shows as `NA` rather than a wrong figure.
`gr_register_model()` fixes that in one line, and its `cached_input_usd` prices
input the provider served from its prompt cache at its own rate. A model with no
cached rate prices cached input as other input.

```{r}
gr_register_model("priced-reasoner", context_window = 128000, max_output = 16000,
                  input_usd = 2, output_usd = 8, reasoning = TRUE)
gr_models()[gr_models()$id %in% c("priced-mock", "priced-reasoner"),
            c("id", "context_window", "reasoning", "input_usd_per_1m", "output_usd_per_1m")]
```

`gr_tokenizer()` says which counter is in use. The default, `"heuristic"`, needs
nothing installed. `gr_set_tokenizer("tiktoken")` switches to OpenAI's own
tokenizer where the reticulate package and Python's `tiktoken` are installed: it
counts in a model's encoding when one is given and otherwise, as the package's
budgets do, in the larger of `cl100k_base` and `o200k_base`. For a model that
is not OpenAI's it is an estimate. Without those packages it stops rather than
falling back, because a silent fallback would change every budget calculation.

`gr_budget()` does the context arithmetic for every request. It cannot return a
non-positive input budget; it raises an error that says what to change instead.
`?gr_options` documents every setting.

```{r include = FALSE}
gr_options(old)
```
